title: b, d, f, l, m, n, p, t, v sound much as in English
body: These letters are close to English. d, t, n and l are made with the tongue against the upper teeth, and l is always the clear “l” of “leaf”, even before a consonant (molto, alto).

title: p, t and k sounds have no puff of air
body: English p, t and k at the start of a syllable come with a small puff of air. Italian p, t and hard c have none, so to English ears they can sound close to b, d and g.

title: a is always “ah”
body: a sounds like the “a” in “father”, never the “a” of “cat” or the weak “uh” of “about”. It keeps its full sound in unstressed and final syllables too: casa ends in a clear “ah”.

title: Most words stress the second-to-last syllable
body: A word with no written accent is usually stressed on its second-to-last syllable. Give that syllable a little more weight and length; the other vowels stay clear and full.

title: e is “eh”, open or closed
body: e sounds like the “e” in “bed”. A stressed e can be open (bene) or closed, nearer the “ay” of “say” without its glide (sera). The spelling does not show which and regions differ, so a clear “eh” is fine. A final e is never silent.

title: o is “oh”, open or closed
body: o is a pure “oh”, without the “w” glide of English “go”. A stressed o can be closed (sono) or open, nearer the “o” of “or” (notte, cosa); the spelling does not show which, and the respellings write both as “oh”. A final o is always a short, clear “oh”.

title: i is “ee”
body: i sounds like the “ee” in “see”, but short, never like the “i” in “sit”. Before another vowel it usually glides into “y”, and after c, g or sc it can be silent (see those rules).

title: r is tapped or rolled with the tongue tip
body: A single r is a quick tap of the tongue tip, like the “tt” in American “better”, or a short trill. rr is a long, strong roll. r is always pronounced, also before a consonant and at the end of a word: parlare, per, terra.

title: Double consonants are held longer
body: A doubled consonant is held for about twice as long, as in “bookcase” or “hot tea”, and the vowel before it is short. It changes meaning: sete (thirst) and sette (seven), caro (dear) and carro (cart).

title: s at the start of a word, before p, t, c, f and as ss is “s”
body: At the start of a word before a vowel, before p, t, hard c, f or q, after a consonant, and doubled as ss, s is always the hissing “s” of “see”: sono, stesso, pensare.

title: c before a, o, u or a consonant is “k”
body: Elsewhere c is a “k” sound, as in “cat”. Before q it simply lengthens the “k” of qu: acqua is “AHK-kwah”.

title: u is “oo”
body: u sounds like the “oo” in “food”, but short, never like the “u” in “but” or “use”. Before another vowel it usually glides into “w” (see that rule).

title: Unstressed i and u before a vowel glide into “y” and “w”
body: An unstressed i or u in front of another vowel joins it in one syllable: ie is “yeh”, ia “yah”, uo “woh”, ua “wah”. When the i or u itself is stressed it stays a full vowel: mio, via, due, tuo, lui, farmacia, polizia.

title: After a, da, è, più and similar words, the next consonant doubles
body: In central and southern Italy, the first consonant of a word is said long after a, da, e, è, o, ma, tra, che, più and other words ending in a stressed vowel. Northern speakers usually do not do this; both are standard.

title: c before e or i sounds like “ch” in “church”
body: Before e or i, c is the “ch” of “church”, and cc is a longer “t-ch” (faccio). Before a, o, u or a consonant it is a hard “k”; to keep it hard before e or i, Italian writes ch.

title: A written accent marks a stressed final vowel
body: Italian writes an accent only when the last vowel of a word is stressed: città, perché, più. On one-syllable words it mostly tells words apart, with no change in sound: è (is) and e (and), sì (yes) and si, là (there) and la.

title: z is “ts” or “dz”
body: z is either “ts” as in “cats” or “dz” as in “adze”; the spelling does not show which, and regions differ. Between vowels a single z is always said long: stazione is “staht-TSYOH-neh”.

title: ch is a hard “k”
body: ch appears only before e or i and is always “k”, never the English “ch”: che is “keh”, chi is “kee”. So sch is “sk”, as in schermo.

title: s between vowels: “z” in the north, “s” further south
body: A single s between vowels is a buzzing “z” in northern Italy and a hissing “s” in much of the centre and south. Both are standard and understood; the respellings here use “z”.

title: h is always silent
body: h is never pronounced. On its own it appears only in forms of avere (ho, hai, ha, hanno) and in foreign words; after c and g it only keeps them hard (che, ghiaccio).

title: g before e or i sounds like “j” in “jam”
body: Before e or i, g is the “j” of “jam”, and gg is a longer “d-j” (oggi). Before a, o, u or a consonant it is hard; to keep it hard before e or i, Italian writes gh.

title: In cia, cio, ciu, gia, gio, giu the i is silent
body: After c, g or sc, an i before a, o or u only shows that the consonant is soft: ciao is “chow”, giorno is “JOHR-noh”. The same is usually true before e (cielo). Only when the i is stressed is it heard: farmacia, bugia.

title: An apostrophe joins two words into one
body: The apostrophe shows a dropped vowel, and the two words are said as one: l'acqua is “LAHK-kwah”, c'è (ci è) is “cheh”. In un po' it marks a shortened word (poco) and adds no sound.

title: g before a, o, u or a consonant is a hard “g”
body: Elsewhere g is the “g” of “go”, including before l in words like inglese. The exceptions are gn and gli, which have sounds of their own.

title: Some words stress the third-to-last syllable
body: Quite a few words are stressed one syllable earlier, and the spelling does not show it, so learn them as you meet them. This includes many verbs ending in -ere (but not avere, vedere, potere) and forms such as erano and vengono.

title: ai, ei, oi, au and eu glide in one syllable
body: When a, e or o comes first, a following i or u is a quick glide in the same syllable: ai is “eye”, ei like “ay” in “day”, oi “oy”, au “ow”, and eu a quick “eh-oo” (euro). Both vowels are heard.

title: qu sounds like “kw”
body: qu is always “kw”, as in “quick”. cu before a vowel has the same sound (cuore, scuola), and cqu is a long “kkw”: acqua is “AHK-kwah”.

title: è is an open “eh”, é a closed one
body: The accent in è marks the open “e” of “bed”: è (is), caffè. The accent in é marks a closed e, a little nearer the “ay” of “say” but without its glide: perché, né. The respellings here write both as “eh”.

title: gli sounds like “lli” in “million”
body: gli is a soft “ly” sound, made with the middle of the tongue against the roof of the mouth. Between vowels it is long, and before another vowel the i is silent: figlio is “FEEL-lyoh”. The word gli (the) is “lyee”.

title: gn sounds like “ny” in “canyon”
body: gn is one sound, like the “ny” in “canyon”, never a “g” followed by “n”. Between vowels it is always long: bagno is “BAHN-nyoh”.

title: sc before e or i sounds like “sh”
body: sce and sci begin with the “sh” of “ship”; before a, o or u the i is silent (lasciare). Between vowels the “sh” is long: pesce. Before a, o, u, h or a consonant, sc is a plain “sk” (scuola, schermo).

title: j, k, w, x and y appear only in foreign words
body: These letters are used only in borrowed words and names, which keep roughly their original sound: weekend, taxi, yogurt. In older Italian names j is “y”: Jacopo.

title: s before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, v sounds like “z”
body: Before these voiced consonants s buzzes like the “z” in “zoo”, also at the start of a word: sveglia is “ZVEHL-lyah”. Before p, t, c, f and q it stays a hissing “s”.

title: gh is a hard “g”
body: gh appears only before e or i and keeps the g hard, as in “get”: colleghi, funghi. It is never the “j” sound.
